title: Celsus’s list of oracles and portents
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς οὕτως ἔχοντα· τί δεῖ καταλέγειν ὅσα ἐκ χρηστηρίων τοῦτο μὲν προφῆται καὶ προφήτιδες τοῦτο δὲ ἄλλοι κάτοχοι καὶ ἄνδρες καὶ γυναῖκες ἐνθέῳ φωνῇ προεῖπον; ὅσα δὲ ἐξ ἀδύτων αὐτῶν ἠκούσθησαν θαυμάσια; ὅσα δὲ ἐξ ἱερείων καὶ θυμάτων τοῖς χρωμένοις ἐδηλώθη, ὅσα δ᾿ ἐξ ἄλλων τεραστίων συμβόλων; τοῖς δ᾿ ἐναργῆ παρέστη φάσματα. μεστὸς τούτων ὁ πᾶς ἐστι βίος. πόσαι μὲν πόλεις ἐκ χρηστηρίων ὠρθώθησαν καὶ νόσους ἀπέθεντο καὶ λιμοὺς, πόσαι δ᾿ ἀμελήσασαι τούτων ἢ ἐκλαθόμεναι κακῶς ἐφθάρησαν; πόσαι δ᾿ εἰς ἀποικίαν ἐστάλησαν καὶ μετελθοῦσαι τὰ προσταχθέντα εὐδαιμόνησαν; πόσοι δυνάσται πόσοι δ᾿ ἰδιῶται παρὰ τοῦτο ἄμεινον ἢ χεῖρον ἀπήλλαξαν; πόσοι μὲν ἀπαιδίας δυσφοροῦντες ὧν ἐδεήθησαν σχόντες [πόσοι] δαιμόνων μῆνιν διέφυγον; πόσοι σωμάτων πηρώσεις ἰάθησαν; πόσοι δ᾿ αὖ πρὸς τοῖς ἱεροῖς ὑβρίσαντες αὐτίκα ἑάλωσαν, οἱ μὲν ἔκφρονες αὐτοῦ ταύτῃ κρατηθέντες οἱ δὲ καὶ ἐξαγγείλαντες (ἃ) ἔδρασαν οἱ δὲ σφᾶς αὐτοὺς διειργασμένοι οἱ δὲ νόσοις ἀνηκέστοις ἐνδεθέντες; ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀδύτων φωνὴ βαρεῖα καθεῖλέν τινας. καὶ οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ταῦτα ὡς ἐναργῆ ὁ Κέλσος προφέρεται καὶ τὰ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν ἀναγεγραμμένα τεράστια. εἴτ᾿ Ἰουδαϊκὰ εἴτε καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, μύθους εἶναι νενόμικε. τί γὰρ οὐχὶ τὰ μὲν ἡμέτερά ἐστιν ἀληθῆ, ἃ (δὲ) λέγει Κέλσος ἀναπλάσματα μυθικά; οἷς οὐδ᾿ Ἑλλήνων φιλόσοφοι αἱρέσεις πεπιστεύκασιν, ὥσπερ ἡ Δημοκρίτου καὶ ἡ Ἐπικούρου καὶ ἡ Ἀριστοτέλους, τάχα ἂν πεπιστευκυῖαι διὰ τὴν ἐνάργειαν τοῖς ἡμετέροις, εἰ παρατετεύχεισαν Μωϋσεῖ ἤ τινι τῶν τὰ παράδοξα ποιησάντων προφητῶν ἢ καὶ αὐτῷ τῷ Ἰησοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see also the next things, which run thus: Why must one list (καταλέγειν) all that from oracles (χρηστηρίων) partly prophets (προφῆται) and prophetesses (προφήτιδες), partly other possessed (κάτοχοι) men and women, foretold (προεῖπον) with inspired voice (ἐνθέῳ φωνῇ)? All the marvels (θαυμάσια) heard from the inner shrines (ἀδύτων) themselves? All revealed (ἐδηλώθη) from victims (ἱερείων) and sacrifices (θυμάτων) to those consulting (χρωμένοις), and all from other portentous signs? To some clear (ἐναργῆ) apparitions (φάσματα) appeared (παρέστη). Full (μεστός) of these is all of life. How many cities were set upright (ὠρθώθησαν) from oracles and put away (ἀπέθεντο) diseases (νόσους) and famines (λιμούς), how many, neglecting (ἀμελήσασαι) or forgetting (ἐκλαθόμεναι) these, were badly destroyed? How many were sent (ἐστάλησαν) to colony (ἀποικίαν) and, pursuing (μετελθοῦσαι) what was commanded, prospered (εὐδαιμόνησαν)? How many rulers (δυνάσται), how many private persons (ἰδιῶται) fared better or worse by this? How many, grieved (δυσφοροῦντες) at childlessness (ἀπαιδίας), having obtained what they asked (ἐδεήθησαν), [how many] escaped the wrath (μῆνιν) of demons? How many were healed of bodily maimings (πηρώσεις)? How many again, having done outrage (ὑβρίσαντες) at the temples, were caught (ἑάλωσαν) at once, some mad (ἔκφρονες) seized right there (αὐτοῦ ταύτῃ), others even announcing what they did, others having made away with themselves, others bound (ἐνδεθέντες) by incurable (ἀνηκέστοις) diseases? Already too from the shrines themselves a heavy voice (φωνὴ βαρεῖα) has brought down (καθεῖλεν) some. And I do not know how Celsus brings forward (προφέρεται) these as evident (ἐναργῆ), and the wonders (τεράστια) recorded among us, whether Jewish or about Jesus and his disciples, has held (νενόμικε) to be myths (μύθους). For why are ours not true, but what Celsus says mythical fabrications? Which not even philosophical schools (αἱρέσεις) of Greeks have believed, such as that of Democritus and of Epicurus and of Aristotle, perhaps having believed ours because of their evidentness (ἐνάργειαν), if they had chanced upon Moses or one of the prophets who did paradoxical things (τὰ παράδοξα) or Jesus himself.
pass_b_english: Let us look also at what comes next, which runs as follows: “Why need I list all that has been foretold with inspired voice, partly from the oracles by prophets and prophetesses, partly by other men and women who were possessed? All the marvels that have been heard from the inner shrines themselves? All that has been made known to inquirers from victims and sacrifices, and all from other portentous signs? To some, clear visions have appeared. All of life is full of these things. How many cities have been restored by oracles and rid themselves of plagues and famines, and how many, by neglecting or forgetting them, have been miserably destroyed? How many have been sent out to found a colony and, by carrying out what was commanded, have prospered? How many rulers, how many private persons, have fared better or worse because of this? How many, distressed at being childless, gained what they prayed for and escaped the wrath of demons? How many have been healed of bodily maiming? How many again, after committing outrage at the temples, were caught at once, some seized with madness on that very spot, others even confessing what they had done, others taking their own lives, others bound fast by incurable diseases? And before now a dreadful voice from the inner shrines themselves has struck some down.”

I do not know how Celsus brings these things forward as clearly true, while he has held that the wonders recorded among us, whether those of the Jews or those about Jesus and his disciples, are myths. Why should ours not be true, and what Celsus tells be fabricated myths? Not even the philosophical schools of the Greeks have believed his stories, such as the schools of Democritus, Epicurus and Aristotle. Yet perhaps they would have believed ours, because of their clear evidence, if they had met Moses, or one of the prophets who worked marvels, or Jesus himself.

choices.choice: The whole first paragraph is Celsus’s text and is put in one set of double quotation marks. ἐκ χρηστηρίων (‘from the oracles’) is taken with the first half, the prophets and prophetesses of the oracle shrines; the possessed men and women are the second half of τοῦτο μὲν ... τοῦτο δέ. ὠρθώθησαν is rendered ‘restored’ (set right, made to prosper), not ‘raised up’, which could be read as ‘founded’. Koetschau brackets the second πόσοι in ‘How many, distressed at childlessness, having gained what they asked, [how many] escaped the wrath of demons’; the bracket is followed, giving one question. If πόσοι is kept, there are two questions (‘gained what they asked? How many escaped the wrath of demons?’). φωνὴ βαρεῖα rendered ‘a dreadful voice’; καθεῖλεν ‘struck down’, which, like the Greek, can mean killed or laid low. ‘His stories’ (οἷς, ‘which’) refers to what Celsus tells; the pronoun is made explicit in English. ἐναργῆ / ἐνάργειαν (‘clear, evident’) is rendered ‘clearly true’ and ‘clear evidence’, keeping Origen’s point that he turns Celsus’s own word back on him. No Scripture is quoted in this chapter.

Opening question: 'foretold ... by oracles, partly by prophets ..., partly by others possessed' made the oracles a third speaker; now 'partly from the oracles by prophets and prophetesses, partly by other men and women who were possessed'
τοῖς χρωμένοις: vague 'those who consult them' changed to 'inquirers'
ὠρθώθησαν: 'raised up' (could mean founded) changed to 'restored'
σφᾶς αὐτοὺς διειργασμένοι: dated 'making away with themselves' changed to 'taking their own lives'
καθεῖλεν: 'struck some dead' (stronger than the Greek) changed to 'struck some down'
Speaker check: the whole first paragraph is Celsus, in one set of quotation marks; Origen's reply follows
